explanation: In tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) deficiency, phenylalanine hydroxylase cannot function, causing phenylalanine accumulation. Treatment involves supplementing L-dopa and 5-hydroxytryptophan (precursors to dopamine and serotonin) since these pathways also require BH4.
keyConcept: BH4 deficiency treated with L-dopa and 5-HTP precursors bypassing the block

explanation: Classic PKU causes deficiency of both catecholamines (due to tyrosine deficiency, the precursor) and melanin (from tyrosine via DOPA oxidase pathway). Tyrosine is an essential dietary requirement in PKU patients.
keyConcept: PKU causes deficiency of both catecholamines and melanin due to tyrosine scarcity

explanation: PKU management requires neonatal screening for early detection, low phenylalanine diet (milk substitutes containing tyrosine), and treatment initiation before one month of age to prevent irreversible brain damage.
keyConcept: PKU management: neonatal screening, low Phe diet, early treatment before 1 month

explanation: Folic acid supplementation (400-800 mcg daily) is recommended for ALL women planning pregnancy to reduce neural tube defect risk in the fetus. This should begin at least one month before conception.
keyConcept: Folic acid supplementation recommended for all women planning pregnancy

explanation: Hyperhomocysteinemia can result from deficiency of vitamin B6 (cystathionine beta-synthase cofactor), B12 (homocysteine to methionine), or folic acid (methyltetrahydrofolate formation). All three vitamins are required for homocysteine metabolism.
keyConcept: Hyperhomocysteinemia from deficiency of B6, B12, or folate (any of the above)

explanation: Folate requirement is 300-400 mcg/day, nearly doubles in the third trimester (400-800 mcg), and is present in leafy vegetables, yeast, and liver. All statements are correct.
keyConcept: Folate: 300-400 mcg/day requirement, doubled in pregnancy, found in leafy vegetables

explanation: The cervical spinal cord has an oval/rounded shape in cross-section due to the enlargement from C5-T1 segments (brachial plexus innervation). The white matter/grey matter ratio increases caudally, not cranially.
keyConcept: Cervical spinal cord is rounded/oval in shape due to cervical enlargement

explanation: Dorsal root ganglia contain nerve cells of variable size (both large light and small dark neurons), not uniform size. The large cells give off heavily myelinated fibers for proprioception; small cells give off lightly myelinated fibers for pain/temperature.
keyConcept: Dorsal root ganglia contain nerve cells of VARIABLE size (not same size) - FALSE

explanation: Dorsal root ganglia are collections of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS (in the PNS), have variable-sized neurons, and are encapsulated by connective tissue. They are not inside the CNS or at viscera.
keyConcept: DRG: outside CNS, variable size neurons, encapsulated connective tissue

explanation: DRG neurons have variable sizes, multiple processes (bipolar or pseudounipolar), and are associated with both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers. They do not all have the same size, and the nucleus is typically central, not eccentric.
keyConcept: DRG neurons: variable size, multiple processes, both myelinated/unmyelinated fibers

explanation: Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's nucleus) gives rise to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (not ventral), located in lamina VII at C8-L3 levels. It has large cells with central nucleus, not eccentric nucleus.
keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus gives rise to DORSAL spinocerebellar tract (not ventral) - FALSE

explanation: Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's nucleus) is NOT present at all spinal levels - it exists only from C8 to L3 segments. The other nuclei (postero-marginal, substantia gelatinosa, main sensory nucleus) are present in all segments.
keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus (C8-L3) is NOT present in all spinal segments - EXCEPTION

explanation: The nucleus dorsalis of Clark projects to the cerebellum via the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, carrying proprioceptive information from muscle spindles and tendon organs. It is in the dorsal horn, present only at certain levels (C8-L3).
keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus projects to cerebellum via dorsal spinocerebellar tract

explanation: The lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) is most prominent at thoracic and upper lumbar levels (T1-L2/3) and contains preganglionic sympathetic neurons (the origin of sympathetic preganglionic fibers).
keyConcept: Lateral horn: origin of preganglionic sympathetic fibers, prominent at thoracic levels

explanation: Destruction of the ventral horn (lower motor neuron) causes flaccid paralysis with muscle atrophy, loss of reflexes, and fasciculations. Crude touch (dorsal column), fine touch (dorsal column), and pain sensation (spinothalamic) are not affected.
keyConcept: Ventral horn destruction causes flaccid paralysis (LMN lesion)

explanation: Grey matter in the spinal cord is located centrally (not outside white matter), composed mainly of nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers. It is surrounded by white matter and contains neuroglia.
keyConcept: Grey matter is centrally located, formed mainly of nerve cells (not outside white matter)

explanation: The anterior horn contains anteromedial, anterolateral, and posterolateral nuclei (the latter two at different cord levels). There is no 'middle' nucleus in the anterior horn - that description is incorrect.
keyConcept: Anterior horn nuclei: anteromedial, anterolateral, posterolateral (no 'middle' nucleus) - EXCEPTION

explanation: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons are located in the intermediolateral cell column of the lateral horn, corresponding to lamina VII of Rexed. Parasympathetic neurons are in sacral segments (S2-S4), not thoracic lamina II.
keyConcept: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons in lateral horn (lamina VII, T1-L2/3)

explanation: The main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius dorsalis) in the posterior horn receives touch and pressure sensations. Substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) processes pain and temperature; posteromarginal nucleus is at the apex.
keyConcept: Main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius) is the primary sensory relay in posterior horn

explanation: The tectospinal tract is present only in upper cervical segments (C1-C6/8), originating from the tectum of midbrain. It does not extend to all spinal cord levels, unlike the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts.
keyConcept: Tectospinal tract does NOT extend to all spinal segments (present only in upper cervical)

explanation: The dorsal (posterior) funiculus contains the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus. The rubrospinal tract is in the lateral funiculus; vestibulospinal tract is in the ventral funiculus.
keyConcept: Cuneate tract (fasciculus cuneatus) lies in the dorsal funiculus

explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract is present in all spinal cord segments, carrying proprioceptive information from lower limbs to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
keyConcept: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract present in all spinal cord segments

explanation: The first-order neuron for proprioception from the lower body has its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion (spinal ganglion). Its central process enters the spinal cord and synapses in the gracile nucleus.
keyConcept: First-order proprioception neuron cell body in dorsal root ganglion

explanation: The second-order neuron for proprioception from the lower body is located in the gracile nucleus on the same side as the entry. Its axon decussates as internal arcuate fibers and ascends in the medial lemniscus.
keyConcept: Second-order proprioception neuron in gracile nucleus of SAME side

explanation: Anterior external arcuate fibers (from the inferior olivary nucleus) relay to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. They carry information that has already decussated at the level of the inferior olivary nucleus.
keyConcept: Anterior external arcuate fibers relay in the inferior olivary nucleus

explanation: Internal arcuate fibers arise from the gracile and cuneate nuclei, decussate (cross the midline) in the medulla, and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the thalamus. They are the second-order neurons of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.
keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers arise from gracile and cuneate nuclei, form medial lemniscus

explanation: The gracile tract (fasciculus gracilis) carries proprioception and fine touch from the lower half of the body, is present in ALL levels of the spinal cord (not just cervical/thoracic), and terminates at the gracile nucleus in the medulla.
keyConcept: Gracile tract: present in ALL levels, carries lower body proprioception to gracile nucleus

explanation: The cuneate tract arises from spinal ganglia of the upper half of the body (above T6), enters the spinal cord, and ascends without crossing to terminate at the cuneate nucleus. The cuneate nucleus is ipsilateral.
keyConcept: Cuneate tract arises from spinal ganglia of upper body, ipsilateral cuneate nucleus

explanation: The central canal is lined by simple columnar to cuboidal epithelium that is partially ciliated (ependymal cells). This is the remnant of the embryonic neural tube lumen.
keyConcept: Central canal lined by simple columnar to cuboidal partially ciliated epithelium (ependymal)

explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm (like astrocytes), while microglia are derived from mesenchyme (monocyte-macrophage lineage). This distinction is important for understanding CNS pathology.
keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes from ectoderm, microglia from mesoderm

explanation: Oligodendrocytes form myelin sheaths in the CNS (one oligodendrocyte myelinates multiple axons). In the PNS, Schwann cells produce myelin. Astrocytes provide structural support; ependymal cells line ventricles.
keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes produce myelin in CNS (Schwann cells in PNS)

explanation: Microglia are the resident phagocytic cells of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in CNS injury and disease, acting as macrophages to clear debris. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are not phagocytic.
keyConcept: Microglia are the phagocytic cells of CNS (mesodermal origin)

explanation: After CNS injury, astrocytes (forming glial scars) and activated microglia (phagocytic response) increase in number. Ependymal cells and oligodendrocytes do not show the same abundance in injury responses.
keyConcept: Astrocytes and microglia are abundant in CNS injury (reactive gliosis)

explanation: Brain capillary endothelial cells have few pinocytic vesicles (not more), abundant mitochondria (for transport functions), tight junctions (not few), and few desmosomes. Tight junctions are essential for the blood-brain barrier function.
keyConcept: Brain endothelium: tight junctions, few pinocytic vesicles (blood-brain barrier)

explanation: Astrocytes (specifically their end-feet) are involved in the blood-brain barrier, induction, and maintenance. They release factors that promote tight junction formation between endothelial cells.
keyConcept: Astrocytes are involved in blood-brain barrier structure and function

explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers; white matter contains myelinated fibers. The distribution of myelin (lipid-rich insulating material) determines the distinction between grey and white matter.
keyConcept: Myelin distribution determines grey vs white matter distribution

explanation: The blood-CSF barrier is formed by tight junctions between ependymal cells lining the ventricles. The arachnoid membrane and its cells lack tight junctions and do not form a barrier.
keyConcept: Tight junctions between ependymal cells form blood-CSF barrier

explanation: Grey matter contains nerve cells, neuroglial cells, and unmyelinated nerve fibers. Myelinated nerve fibers are characteristic of white matter, not grey matter.
keyConcept: Myelinated nerve fibers are NOT present in grey matter (white matter characteristic) - EXCEPTION

explanation: Protoplasmic astrocytes (found in grey matter) have numerous short, branching processes. Fibrous astrocytes (found in white matter) have few long, thin processes.
keyConcept: Protoplasmic astrocytes: numerous short branching processes (grey matter)

explanation: Tanycytes are specialized ependymal cells that line the floor of the third ventricle, particularly in the infundibular recess. They have long basal processes and are thought to transport substances between the ventricle and hypothalamic nuclei.
keyConcept: Tanycytes line the third ventricle floor, involved in neuroendocrine transport
